blocks.prompt: The Lady with the Lamp
blocks.text: A nurse is a person whose job is to care for people who are sick, hurt, or getting better. Nurses do far more than hand out medicine. They watch a patient closely and notice small changes, like a fever rising or a wound that is not healing well. To do this, a nurse checks what doctors call vital signs. These are your temperature, your pulse, how fast you breathe, and your blood pressure. Together they tell a nurse how your body is doing. Long ago, hospitals were dirty and crowded, and many patients did not get better. Then a woman named Florence Nightingale changed everything. During a war in the 1850s, she cleaned the wards, opened the windows, and made sure everyone washed. Far fewer soldiers died. At night she walked the rows of beds carrying a lamp, so people called her the Lady with the Lamp. Because of her, nursing became a respected job all around the world.

blocks.prompt: The People Who Stay at Your Side
blocks.text: Most people meet a nurse before they ever meet a doctor. Nurses are the health workers who spend the most time at a patient's side, and there are more of them than any other kind of health worker on Earth. Their job is to watch, to care, and to catch problems early. A nurse is trained to read the body's signals. By checking a patient's temperature, pulse, breathing, and blood pressure, a nurse can tell whether someone is improving or getting worse, often before the patient feels the change. A good nurse also listens. A frightened child or a worried grandparent calms down faster when someone explains, gently, what is about to happen. Modern nursing grew out of the work of two women in the 1850s. Florence Nightingale, an English nurse, transformed filthy war hospitals by demanding clean water, fresh air, and constant handwashing, and the number of deaths dropped sharply. At the same time, a Jamaican-British nurse named Mary Seacole used her own money to travel to the same war and care for soldiers near the battlefield. Both proved that skilled, organized care saves lives. Nursing is not one job but many. A pediatric nurse cares for children. An emergency nurse handles accidents and sudden illness. A school nurse looks after students during the day, and a midwife helps mothers bring new babies safely into the world. Whatever the setting, the heart of the work is the same: pay close attention, act quickly, and treat every patient with kindness.

blocks.prompt: The Watchers at the Bedside
blocks.text: Walk into any hospital and the person who greets you, weighs you, checks your pulse, and stays with you through the long night is almost always a nurse. Nurses make up the largest single group of health workers in the world, and in most countries they provide the majority of hands-on care. Doctors diagnose and prescribe, but nurses are the ones who watch a patient hour by hour and notice when something quietly goes wrong. That watching is a skill built on measurement. A nurse tracks four vital signs: body temperature, pulse, breathing rate, and blood pressure. Each one is a window into the body. A climbing temperature can mean infection. A racing pulse can mean pain, fear, or blood loss. Read together and over time, these numbers let a nurse spot trouble long before it becomes an emergency, which is why hospitals record them again and again. The profession as we know it was shaped in the 1850s, during the Crimean War. Florence Nightingale arrived at a British army hospital where more soldiers were dying of infection than of their wounds. She insisted on clean linen, fresh air, decent food, and relentless handwashing, and the death rate fell dramatically. Afterward she used careful records and statistics to prove that hygiene saves lives, and she founded the first modern nursing school. Working through the same war, Mary Seacole, a Jamaican-British healer, funded her own journey and set up a lodging house near the front to nurse wounded men. Between them they turned nursing from unskilled labor into a trained, respected profession. Today nursing has branched into dozens of specialties, from caring for newborns to guiding families through their final days. The tools have changed and the science has deepened, but the core has not. A nurse is the person who stays, who watches, and who treats the patient as a person and not just a problem to be solved.

blocks.prompt: The Quiet Profession That Holds the Room
blocks.text: There is a good chance that the first medical professional you ever met was a nurse, and an even better chance that a nurse, not a doctor, spent the most time keeping you safe. Nurses are the largest group of health workers on the planet, and in hospital after hospital they carry out the quiet, continuous work on which everything else depends. A surgeon may spend two hours on an operation. A nurse spends the following two weeks making sure the patient actually recovers. The heart of nursing is careful observation turned into action. A nurse learns to read the body through its vital signs: temperature, pulse, breathing rate, and blood pressure. These four numbers seem simple, yet in combination they form a kind of early warning system. A slight fever paired with a fast heartbeat and shallow breathing may mean nothing on its own, but a nurse trained to see patterns recognizes the shape of an infection taking hold and acts before the patient is in danger. This is why the same measurements are taken over and over. A single reading is a snapshot. A series of readings tells a story. That combination of watchfulness and cleanliness is exactly what turned nursing into a modern profession. In the 1850s, during the Crimean War, a British nurse named Florence Nightingale found a military hospital where filth and crowding were killing more soldiers than enemy fire. She demanded clean water, open windows, proper food, and constant handwashing, and the death rate collapsed. Crucially, she did not simply trust that it worked. She kept meticulous records and used statistics and clear diagrams to prove that hygiene saved lives, an argument that convinced governments to change how hospitals were run. She became known as the Lady with the Lamp for her nightly rounds among the wounded. In the same war, a Jamaican-British woman named Mary Seacole, refused an official nursing post, paid her own way to the front and built a lodging house where she treated sick and injured soldiers. For a long time her contribution was nearly forgotten, and only recently has she been widely honored alongside Nightingale. Modern nursing has since divided into a remarkable range of specialties. A neonatal nurse may care for a baby smaller than a hand, while a hospice nurse helps a dying person spend their last days in comfort and dignity. There are nurses in emergency rooms, in schools, in remote villages, and on the phone giving advice at midnight. What unites them is not a single set of tasks but a single stance toward other people: pay attention, stay close, and never treat a patient as merely a case. It is worth noticing how much of this rests on trust rather than technology. The stethoscope and the thermometer matter, but the reason a frightened patient calms down is that a competent, steady person has chosen to stay in the room. That is the part of nursing no machine has replaced, and probably none ever will.
